clue.text: Caretaker's rent reduced after New Year's Day

indicators.note: something reduced has been cut down, so a letter is trimmed from the end
one piece placed after another simply follows it in the line

parts.note: the first day of the year is 1 January, written JAN plus the Roman numeral I
rent is the past participle of rend, meaning torn

explanation.surface: A caretaker's rent is cut after the New Year holiday.
explanation.walkthrough: 'rent' looks like money paid to a landlord, but it is the past tense of the old verb rend, to rip. New Year's Day is written as the date: month abbreviation plus Roman one.
explanation.definitionFit: A janitor looks after a building, cleaning and maintaining it, which is exactly what a caretaker does.

clue.text: Hotel offering British journo large drink at entrance

indicators.note: standing at the entrance means coming first, so this piece leads the line

parts.note: a double is a twice-sized measure of spirits
standard abbreviation for British
ED, short for editor, is the usual crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A hotel treats a British reporter to a big drink as they arrive.
explanation.walkthrough: The drink is read in the clue after B and ED, but 'at entrance' moves it to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Hotels advertise rooms by bed type, and a bed for two sleepers is one thing a hotel offers its guests.

clue.text: Scarf — top of neck is hot

parts.note: a stole is a long scarf worn over the shoulders

indicators.note: the top of a down entry word is its first letter, so only the opening letter is kept

parts.note: first letter of neck

explanation.surface: A scarf keeps the neck warm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hot' looks like temperature, matching scarf and neck, but it is slang for stolen goods.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is informal slang for goods that have been taken illegally and are still easy for police to trace.

clue.text: Nun hiding — is a church in trouble

indicators.note: to hide something is to keep it inside, so one piece goes within another

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
CE is the Church of England

explanation.surface: A nun goes into hiding because a church is in trouble.
explanation.walkthrough: The nun is not a person to find but letters to split around 'is a'; the Church of England, abbreviated, follows.
explanation.definitionFit: A nuisance is something that causes annoyance or bother, so it serves as a noun for trouble.

clue.text: Place where police found clue to dastardly con

parts.note: the answer's first word is the instruction: a new version of what follows

indicators.note: the answer itself is offered as a clue that describes a rearranged version of these words

parts.note: taken as written; twelve letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: Detectives turned up a lead on a wicked swindle.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read NEW SCOTLAND YARD as 'a new arrangement of SCOTLAND YARD', and that new arrangement is DASTARDLY CON. New Scotland Yard is the London Metropolitan Police headquarters.
explanation.definitionFit: New Scotland Yard is the headquarters building of London's Metropolitan Police, so officers are located there.

clue.text: Man's man, for example

parts.note: surface reading: a man's man, a sociable, hearty chap
setter's reading: Man is the Isle of Man, so a man belonging to it is one of its inhabitants

explanation.walkthrough: The capital M is the giveaway: Man is the Isle of Man in the Irish Sea, and a Manxman is an example of someone from an island.
explanation.definitionFit: Anyone living on an island such as the Isle of Man is an inhabitant of that island.

clue.text: American spy avoiding university town

parts.note: standard abbreviation for American

indicators.note: something avoiding a thing keeps clear of it, so that letter is left out

parts.note: a scout is sent ahead to spy
standard abbreviation for university

explanation.surface: An American agent stays away from a college town.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove U from SCOUT and put A in front. Ascot is a town in Berkshire, England, famous for its racecourse.
explanation.definitionFit: Ascot is a small English town west of London, best known for hosting Royal Ascot horse racing.

clue.text: Friendly drink

definitions.meaning: first meaning: warm and polite in manner
second meaning: a sweet fruit syrup diluted to drink

explanation.walkthrough: It reads like an invitation for a sociable pint, but the two words are separate meanings.
explanation.definitionFit: As an adjective it describes warm, genial relations; as a noun it is a concentrated fruit squash.

clue.text: Newspaper exposed Stew

parts.note: a rag is a disparaging word for a newspaper
out means revealed, made public

explanation.surface: A tabloid lays bare a scandal about someone called Stew.
explanation.walkthrough: The capital S of 'Stew' dresses it as a man's name; it is the dish being defined.
explanation.definitionFit: A ragout is a French-style slow-cooked dish of meat and vegetables in sauce, a kind of casserole.

clue.text: Player invited to compete is unbroken facing deuce?

indicators.note: pieces facing each other sit side by side, so one is set next to the other

parts.note: an unbroken horse has not been tamed, so it is wild
a deuce is the two in a pack of cards

explanation.surface: A tennis invitee is still unbeaten when the score reaches deuce.
explanation.walkthrough: Tennis words — unbroken serve, deuce — paint the match, but deuce is a playing card and unbroken describes an untamed horse.
explanation.definitionFit: In tennis a wild card is an entrant admitted to a tournament without qualifying, at the organisers' discretion.

clue.text: Dogs graffiti artist Rob conclusively draws outside

indicators.note: drawing something from outside means it surrounds the rest

parts.note: to draw is to pull

indicators.note: conclusively means at the conclusion, so only each word's final letter is kept

parts.note: last letters of the three words

explanation.surface: A street artist called Rob finally sketches dogs on a wall.
explanation.walkthrough: 'conclusively' takes the last letter of all three words before it, not just Rob; those three sit inside P-ULLS.
explanation.definitionFit: Pit bulls are a muscular terrier breed originally bred for fighting, so they are a type of dog.

clue.text: Idiot getting money back with it

indicators.note: going back means travelling the wrong way, so these letters run right to left

parts.note: tin is old slang for money
W is the abbreviation for with
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fool gets a refund and somehow keeps it.
explanation.walkthrough: TIN is British slang for cash.
explanation.definitionFit: Nitwit is a mild, informal insult for a silly or stupid person, the same as a fool.

clue.text: Doctor, doctor — who let mine be born?

indicators.note: to doctor something is to tamper with it, so the letters get altered

parts.note: taken as written, sixteen letters

explanation.surface: A 'Doctor, doctor' joke about a doctor who delivers a baby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Doctor, doctor' sets up the old joke format, but the first Doctor is the instruction and the second is part of the letters, along with 'who let mine'.
explanation.definitionFit: To come into the world is an idiom for birth, the moment a baby arrives.

clue.text: See 12
Aware of travelling to hen party

indicators.note: things travelling are on the move, so the letters move around

parts.note: taken as written
a ball is a formal dance party

explanation.surface: Someone knows about a trip to a hen party.
explanation.walkthrough: 'hen party' looks like one unit, a pre-wedding celebration, but 'hen' joins 'to' as letters and 'party' stands alone. A hen party is the British name for a bachelorette party.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on the ball is an idiom for being alert, quick and well informed about what is going on.

clue.text: Son with top tip — it helps manage leaks

parts.note: standard abbreviation for son
taken as written
to cock is to tilt or tip, as a hat

explanation.surface: A son gets a top tip about something that controls leaks — perhaps about a leaky secret.
explanation.walkthrough: 'top tip' reads as good advice, but 'tip' means tilt.
explanation.definitionFit: A stopcock is the valve on a water pipe that is turned off to halt the supply when a pipe springs a leak.

clue.text: When rejected, Yellowcoat Ted never harbours bad blood

indicators.note: rejected things are sent back, so the letters run the other way
to harbour is to shelter within, so the letters are concealed inside the words

parts.note: letters spanning the end of the first word, all of the second and start of the third

explanation.surface: A rejected holiday-camp entertainer, Ted, never lets go of a grudge.
explanation.walkthrough: A Yellowcoat is a Pontins holiday-camp entertainer in Britain. Read the run of letters from right to left.
explanation.definitionFit: A vendetta is a long feud, and bad blood is an idiom for lasting hostility between people.

clue.text: Musk penning letter to Aristotle — and another

indicators.note: to pen is to enclose, as animals in a pen, so one piece is shut inside another

parts.note: Elon Musk, the tech billionaire
a Greek letter, as Aristotle would have written

explanation.surface: Elon Musk writes a letter to Aristotle, and then another.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' suggests writing, but it means enclosing. 'another' means another Greek letter, carried over from the letter to Aristotle.
explanation.definitionFit: Epsilon is the fifth character of the Greek alphabet, so it is a second example of the same kind as psi.

clue.text: Failure of almost all arson, incredibly

indicators.note: almost means not quite complete, so the final letter is lost

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: something done incredibly is beyond belief, so the letters end up in an unbelievable order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Nearly every attempt at arson failed, unbelievably.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Failure of' looks like it introduces whose failure, but 'of' only joins definition to wordplay. An also-ran comes from horse racing.
explanation.definitionFit: An also-ran is a horse that finishes out of the places, hence any loser or unsuccessful person.

clue.text: Case for Hazel, say, to have lines after she pursues group of teachers once

indicators.note: one who pursues comes behind, so this piece follows the earlier one
placed after means coming later in the line

parts.note: the NUT was the National Union of Teachers, merged in 2017
taken as written
L is the abbreviation for line, doubled for lines

explanation.surface: A woman called Hazel has a legal case, and must write lines after chasing a group of teachers.
explanation.walkthrough: Hazel looks like a woman's name at the start of a sentence; it is the hazel tree, whose nut is the 'say'. The NUT (National Union of Teachers) no longer exists, hence 'once'.
explanation.definitionFit: A hazelnut is one example of a nut, and the hard outer casing enclosing its kernel is its shell.

clue.text: Stupor caused by knight taking smack? Quite the reverse

indicators.note: taking something in means holding it, so one piece goes inside another
this swaps which piece holds and which is held from what the sentence first said

parts.note: a smack is a slight taste or hint, a trace
N is the chess notation for knight

explanation.surface: A daze brought on by a knight being slapped.
explanation.walkthrough: As written the knight takes the smack; 'Quite the reverse' flips it so the smack takes the knight. Smack here is a trace or taste, as in 'a smack of garlic', not a blow.
explanation.definitionFit: A trance is a half-conscious, dazed state, close in sense to a stupor in which one barely responds.

clue.text: Jumble sale occasionally helps out

indicators.note: to jumble is to mix up, so the letters are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: occasionally means now and then, so every other letter is picked

parts.note: second and fourth letters

explanation.surface: Now and then a jumble sale lends a hand.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumble sale' reads as one thing, a charity sale of donated goods, but 'Jumble' is the instruction and 'sale' the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Out is informal for unconscious or sleeping, as in 'out like a light'.

clue.text: More out of context rants

indicators.note: taken out of something means drawn from within it, so the letters lie inside the words

parts.note: letters across the end of the first word and start of the second

explanation.surface: Further rants quoted out of context.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out of context' is a set phrase, but 'out of' points to letters inside 'context rants'.
explanation.definitionFit: Extra means additional, an amount beyond the usual, so it can stand in for more.

clue.text: Publication of article on playing chess — essentially rook captures bishop

indicators.note: a piece that captures another takes it in, holding it inside
one piece on another in an across entry comes right after it
the essence of something is its core, so only the central letter is kept

parts.note: middle letter of a seven-letter word
middle letter of a five-letter word
the indefinite article
taken as written
B is the chess notation for bishop

explanation.surface: An article about chess play, in which a rook takes a bishop.
explanation.walkthrough: 'essentially' applies to both 'playing' and 'chess', giving their middle letters; the A sits on them, and ROOK opens to take in B after its R.
explanation.definitionFit: A yearbook is an annual publication, such as a school's record or an almanac of the year's events.

clue.text: Abundance provided by Norse god through prayer

indicators.note: something passing through another runs inside it, so one piece is placed within

parts.note: a plea is an earnest request, a prayer
Thor is the Norse god of thunder

explanation.surface: A Norse god answers a prayer with plenty.
explanation.walkthrough: 'through prayer' sounds like by means of praying, but it means the god goes through, inside, PLEA.
explanation.definitionFit: A plethora is an excess or great quantity of something, so it matches abundance as a noun.

clue.text: Stock of wine retailer picked up

indicators.note: sounds picked up are heard, so the word is judged by how it is spoken

parts.note: a retailer is someone who sells

explanation.surface: A wine merchant's stock is collected.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Stock of wine retailer' reads as one phrase, a merchant's goods; the definition stops at 'wine'.
explanation.definitionFit: A cellar can mean a person's collection of wines, as in 'he keeps a fine cellar', not just the room.

clue.text: Immaculate header from Uruguay devastated Denmark

indicators.note: the header of a word is its head, the first letter

parts.note: first letter of the country

indicators.note: something devastated is wrecked, so the letters are left in ruins and reordered

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A perfect header by Uruguay crushes Denmark in a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'header' looks like a football header, but it signals the first letter of Uruguay.
explanation.definitionFit: Unmarked means free of stains or blemishes, which matches spotless or pristine, the sense of immaculate.
